claim: The hypothalamic ventral premammillary nucleus (PMv) is a glutamatergic nucleus essential for the metabolic control of reproduction.
source: The hypothalamic ventral premammillary nucleus (PMv) is a glutamatergic nucleus essential for the metabolic control of reproduction.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about the PMv.

claim: Conditional deletion of leptin receptor long form (LepRb) in vesicular glutamate transporter 2 (Vglut2) expressing neurons results in virtually no reproductive deficits.
source: However, conditional deletion of leptin receptor long form (LepRb) in vesicular glutamate transporter 2 (Vglut2) expressing neurons results in virtually no reproductive deficits.
evidence: This statement references prior findings that are cited in the introduction (Martin et al., 2014; Zuure et al., 2013).

claim: LH level increased in animals correctly targeted to the PMv following chemogenetic stimulation.
source: LH level increased in animals correctly targeted to the PMv, and LH level was correlated to the number of Fos immunoreactive neurons in the PMv.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: LH level was correlated to the number of Fos immunoreactive neurons in the PMv.
source: LH level increased in animals correctly targeted to the PMv, and LH level was correlated to the number of Fos immunoreactive neurons in the PMv.
evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 1H with statistical analysis (Pearson r = 0.67; p = 0.0007).

claim: LeprΔVGlut2 females showed delayed age of puberty.
source: Next, females with deletion of Slc17a6 (Vglut2) in LepRb neurons (LeprΔVGlut2) showed delayed age of puberty, disrupted estrous cycles, increased gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) concentration in the axon terminals, and disrupted LH secretion, suggesting impaired GnRH release.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5C showing delayed first estrus.

claim: LeprΔVGlut2 females showed disrupted estrous cycles.
source: Next, females with deletion of Slc17a6 (Vglut2) in LepRb neurons (LeprΔVGlut2) showed delayed age of puberty, disrupted estrous cycles, increased gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) concentration in the axon terminals, and disrupted LH secretion, suggesting impaired GnRH release.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5G-J showing longer cycle duration and altered time in cycle phases.

claim: LeprΔVGlut2 females showed increased gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) concentration in the axon terminals.
source: Next, females with deletion of Slc17a6 (Vglut2) in LepRb neurons (LeprΔVGlut2) showed delayed age of puberty, disrupted estrous cycles, increased gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) concentration in the axon terminals, and disrupted LH secretion, suggesting impaired GnRH release.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6A-C showing increased GnRH-ir integrated density in the Arc.

claim: LeprΔVGlut2 females showed disrupted LH secretion.
source: Next, females with deletion of Slc17a6 (Vglut2) in LepRb neurons (LeprΔVGlut2) showed delayed age of puberty, disrupted estrous cycles, increased gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) concentration in the axon terminals, and disrupted LH secretion, suggesting impaired GnRH release.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6E-F showing reduced LH response to kisspeptin.

claim: The disrupted LH secretion in LeprΔVGlut2 females suggests impaired GnRH release.
source: Next, females with deletion of Slc17a6 (Vglut2) in LepRb neurons (LeprΔVGlut2) showed delayed age of puberty, disrupted estrous cycles, increased gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) concentration in the axon terminals, and disrupted LH secretion, suggesting impaired GnRH release.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed data of increased GnRH at terminals and reduced LH response.

claim: Deletion of Vglut2 in PMv neurons blocked leptin-induced pubertal development in LepR-null mice.
source: Control LeprloxTB mice with PMv LepRb rescue showed vaginal opening, follicle maturation, and became pregnant, while LeprloxTB;Vglut2flox mice showed no pubertal development.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7 showing lack of vaginal opening, uterine growth, and corpora lutea in LeprloxTB;Vglut2flox mice with AAV-Cre.

claim: Glutamatergic neurotransmission from leptin sensitive neurons regulates the reproductive axis.
source: Our results indicate that glutamatergic neurotransmission from leptin sensitive neurons regulates the reproductive axis, and that leptin action on pubertal development via PMv neurons requires Vglut2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Leptin action on pubertal development via PMv neurons requires Vglut2.
source: Our results indicate that glutamatergic neurotransmission from leptin sensitive neurons regulates the reproductive axis, and that leptin action on pubertal development via PMv neurons requires Vglut2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiment data in Figure 7.

claim: Food scarcity leads to suppression of fertility.
source: Food scarcity leads to suppression of fertility (Ahima et al., 1996; Bronson and Marsteller, 1985; Cagampang et al., 1990; Cameron et al., 1991; Parfitt et al., 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Excess adiposity may induce ovulatory dysfunction.
source: Similarly, excess adiposity may induce ovulatory dysfunction, higher risks of pregnancy complications and earlier age at puberty onset (Biro et al., 2006; Burt Solorzano and McCartney, 2010; Mahany et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Excess adiposity may cause higher risks of pregnancy complications.
source: Similarly, excess adiposity may induce ovulatory dysfunction, higher risks of pregnancy complications and earlier age at puberty onset (Biro et al., 2006; Burt Solorzano and McCartney, 2010; Mahany et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Excess adiposity may cause earlier age at puberty onset.
source: Similarly, excess adiposity may induce ovulatory dysfunction, higher risks of pregnancy complications and earlier age at puberty onset (Biro et al., 2006; Burt Solorzano and McCartney, 2010; Mahany et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mice and humans with mutations in the leptin or leptin receptor genes are infertile.
source: Mice and humans with mutations in the leptin or leptin receptor genes are infertile and remain in a prepubertal state (Bray and York, 1979; Farooqi et al., 2007; Farooqi et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mice and humans with mutations in the leptin or leptin receptor genes remain in a prepubertal state.
source: Mice and humans with mutations in the leptin or leptin receptor genes are infertile and remain in a prepubertal state (Bray and York, 1979; Farooqi et al., 2007; Farooqi et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Specific restoration of the leptin receptor (Lepr) gene only in neurons of Lepr-deficient mice rescues infertility.
source: Specific restoration of the leptin receptor (Lepr) gene only in neurons of Lepr-deficient mice rescues infertility (de Luca et al., 2005; Quennell et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: GnRH neurons do not express Lepr.
source: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) neurons do not express Lepr (Quennell et al., 2009) but they do receive direct innervation from Lepr-expressing neurons (Louis et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: GnRH neurons receive direct innervation from Lepr-expressing neurons.
source: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) neurons do not express Lepr (Quennell et al., 2009) but they do receive direct innervation from Lepr-expressing neurons (Louis et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The ventral premammillary nucleus (PMv) is rich in neurons expressing the long form of LepR (LepRb).
source: An often-overlooked hypothalamic site, rich in neurons expressing the long form of LepR (LepRb), is the ventral premammillary nucleus (PMv) (Donato et al., 2011; Han et al., 2020; Leshan et al., 2009; Louis et al., 2011; Ross et al., 2018; Scott et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Bilateral lesions of the PMv disrupt estrous cycles in rats.
source: In rats, bilateral lesions of the PMv disrupt estrous cycles and the ability of leptin to increase luteinizing hormone (LH) secretion following a fast (Donato et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Bilateral lesions of the PMv disrupt the ability of leptin to increase luteinizing hormone (LH) secretion following a fast in rats.
source: In rats, bilateral lesions of the PMv disrupt estrous cycles and the ability of leptin to increase luteinizing hormone (LH) secretion following a fast (Donato et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Endogenous restoration of LepRb exclusively in PMv neurons rescues pubertal maturation and fertility in Lepr-null female mice.
source: Endogenous restoration of LepRb exclusively in PMv neurons rescues pubertal maturation and fertility in Lepr-null female mice (Donato et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Leptin responsive neurons in the PMv project directly to and make contacts with GnRH cell bodies.
source: Leptin responsive neurons in the PMv project directly to and make contacts with GnRH cell bodies and their terminals in the adjacencies of the median eminence (Boehm et al., 2005; Canteras et al., 1992; Donato et al., 2011; Leshan et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Leptin responsive neurons in the PMv project directly to and make contacts with GnRH terminals in the adjacencies of the median eminence.
source: Leptin responsive neurons in the PMv project directly to and make contacts with GnRH cell bodies and their terminals in the adjacencies of the median eminence (Boehm et al., 2005; Canteras et al., 1992; Donato et al., 2011; Leshan et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: PMv neurons project to the anteroventral periventricular (AVPV) and arcuate (Arc) nuclei.
source: These cells also project to the anteroventral periventricular (AVPV) and arcuate (Arc) nuclei, home of kisspeptin (Kiss1 gene) neurons, the main GnRH regulatory population (Canteras et al., 1992; Donato et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Kisspeptin neurons are the main GnRH regulatory population.
source: These cells also project to the anteroventral periventricular (AVPV) and arcuate (Arc) nuclei, home of kisspeptin (Kiss1 gene) neurons, the main GnRH regulatory population (Canteras et al., 1992; Donato et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Projections from the PMv make apparent contacts with Kiss1 expressing cells in the AVPV.
source: Projections from the PMv make apparent contacts with Kiss1 expressing cells in the AVPV (Donato et al., 2011), and stimulation of PMv neurons directly activates kisspeptin cells in both the AVPV and the Arc (Ross et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Stimulation of PMv neurons directly activates kisspeptin cells in both the AVPV and the Arc.
source: Projections from the PMv make apparent contacts with Kiss1 expressing cells in the AVPV (Donato et al., 2011), and stimulation of PMv neurons directly activates kisspeptin cells in both the AVPV and the Arc (Ross et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The PMv is essentially glutamatergic.
source: The PMv is essentially glutamatergic (Vong et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: LepRb neurons coexpress the vesicular glutamate transporter Slc17a6 (Vglut2).
source: LepRb neurons coexpress the vesicular glutamate transporter Slc17a6 (Vglut2) (Donato et al., 2011), and acute administration of leptin depolarizes most of these neurons (Williams et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Acute administration of leptin depolarizes most PMv LepRb neurons.
source: LepRb neurons coexpress the vesicular glutamate transporter Slc17a6 (Vglut2) (Donato et al., 2011), and acute administration of leptin depolarizes most of these neurons (Williams et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Glutamatergic terminals are abundant in GnRH neurons.
source: Glutamatergic terminals are abundant in GnRH (Moore et al., 2018; Yeo et al., 2021) and in kisspeptin (Porter et al., 2021) neurons, while states of low leptin levels, as in fasting, reduce the number of glutamatergic synaptic inputs to kisspeptin neurons of male macaques (Shamas et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Glutamatergic terminals are abundant in kisspeptin neurons.
source: Glutamatergic terminals are abundant in GnRH (Moore et al., 2018; Yeo et al., 2021) and in kisspeptin (Porter et al., 2021) neurons, while states of low leptin levels, as in fasting, reduce the number of glutamatergic synaptic inputs to kisspeptin neurons of male macaques (Shamas et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: States of low leptin levels, as in fasting, reduce the number of glutamatergic synaptic inputs to kisspeptin neurons of male macaques.
source: Glutamatergic terminals are abundant in GnRH (Moore et al., 2018; Yeo et al., 2021) and in kisspeptin (Porter et al., 2021) neurons, while states of low leptin levels, as in fasting, reduce the number of glutamatergic synaptic inputs to kisspeptin neurons of male macaques (Shamas et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Congenital deletion of Lepr in glutamatergic neurons has virtually no effect on pubertal development or reproductive function.
source: Prior data, however, have shown that congenital deletion of Lepr in glutamatergic neurons has virtually no effect on pubertal development or reproductive function (Martin et al., 2014; Zuure et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: About 55% (8/15) of mice with unilateral AAV-hM3Dq centered in the PMv showed an increase in LH release above 0.5 ng/ml within 10–20 min following the CNO injection.
source: About 55% (8/15) of mice with unilateral AAV-hM3Dq centered in the PMv showed an increase in LH release above 0.5 ng/ml within 10–20 min following the CNO injection (0.65–3.11 ng/ml).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data from the chemogenetic activation study.

claim: The positive AUC for the PMv-hit with LH increase group was significantly different from 0.
source: The positive AUC for the PMv-hit with LH increase group was significantly different from 0, indicating a significant rise in LH levels during this time, while the positive AUC in the other groups did not differ from 0 indicating that LH did not increase following the injection (Figure 1E, F).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The positive AUC in control groups did not differ from 0 indicating that LH did not increase following the injection.
source: The positive AUC for the PMv-hit with LH increase group was significantly different from 0, indicating a significant rise in LH levels during this time, while the positive AUC in the other groups did not differ from 0 indicating that LH did not increase following the injection (Figure 1E, F).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The number of Fos-ir neurons per section in the PMv was higher in PMv-hits that showed increased LH, than in animals that showed no LH increase and in negative controls.
source: The number of Fos-ir neurons per section in the PMv was variable between groups, with higher number of Fos-ir neurons observed in PMv-hits that showed increased LH, than in animals that showed no LH increase and in negative controls (PMv-misses and AAV-mCherry combined) (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Peak LH levels (ng/ml) were positively correlated to the number of Fos-ir neurons in the PMv.
source: Peak LH levels (ng/ml) were positively correlated to the number of Fos-ir neurons in the PMv, suggesting a link between stimulation of LepRb neurons in the PMv and induction of LH release (Figure 1H).
evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 1H with statistical analysis (Pearson r = 0.67; p = 0.0007).

claim: There is a link between stimulation of LepRb neurons in the PMv and induction of LH release.
source: Peak LH levels (ng/ml) were positively correlated to the number of Fos-ir neurons in the PMv, suggesting a link between stimulation of LepRb neurons in the PMv and induction of LH release (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: There is a threshold in which a number or a subset of PMv LepRb is necessary for successful stimulation of LH secretion.
source: It also suggests that there is a threshold in which a number or a subset of PMv LepRb is necessary for successful stimulation of LH secretion.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only animals with sufficient Fos activation showed LH increase.

claim: All mice with AAV-hM3Dq targeting the PMv and injected with clozapine showed an increase in LH 10 min after the injection.
source: All mice with AAV-hM3Dq targeting the PMv (Fos-ir) and injected with clozapine also showed an increase in LH 10 min after the injection (0.87–1.18 ng/ml, Figure 2A, B), whereas two out of seven (28.5 %) control mice with no AAV showed an increase in LH following the clozapine injection (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Two out of seven (28.5%) control mice with no AAV showed an increase in LH following the clozapine injection.
source: All mice with AAV-hM3Dq targeting the PMv (Fos-ir) and injected with clozapine also showed an increase in LH 10 min after the injection (0.87–1.18 ng/ml, Figure 2A, B), whereas two out of seven (28.5 %) control mice with no AAV showed an increase in LH following the clozapine injection (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The positive AUC between −10 to 20 min showed a significant increase in LH levels in the clozapine AAV-hM3Dq group, but not in the group with no AAV.
source: The positive AUC between −10 to 20 min showed a significant increase in LH levels in the clozapine AAV-hM3Dq group, but not in the group with no AAV (Figure 2D, E).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The number of Fos-ir neurons per section in the PMv was higher in animals with hM3Dq than in those with no AAV.
source: The number of Fos-ir neurons per section in the PMv was higher in animals with hM3Dq than in those with no AAV, in which virtually no Fos-ir cells were observed (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The total number of neurons coexpressing both Fos- and mCherry-ir per section in the posterior Arc was higher in PMv-hit animals than in negative control animals.
source: The total number of neurons coexpressing both Fos- and mCherry-ir per section in the posterior Arc was higher in PMv-hit animals, whether they showed an increase in LH, than in negative control animals (PMv-miss and AAV-mCherry combined) (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Peak LH levels were positively correlated to the number of Fos-ir + mCherry ir neurons in the Arc.
source: As observed for the PMv, peak LH levels were positively correlated to the number of Fos-ir + mCherry ir neurons in the Arc (Figure 3D), but not with the total number of Fos-ir neurons alone in the Arc (r = 0.3; p = 0.16).
evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 3D with statistical analysis (Pearson r = 0.62; p = 0.002).

claim: Peak LH levels were not correlated with the total number of Fos-ir neurons alone in the Arc.
source: As observed for the PMv, peak LH levels were positively correlated to the number of Fos-ir + mCherry ir neurons in the Arc (Figure 3D), but not with the total number of Fos-ir neurons alone in the Arc (r = 0.3; p = 0.16).
evidence: This is stated with statistical values (r = 0.3; p = 0.16).

claim: LepRb-expressing neurons in the Arc may have contributed to the increase in LH observed following CNO treatment.
source: This observation suggested that LepRb-expressing neurons in the Arc may have contributed to the increase in LH observed following CNO treatment.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between Arc mCherry/Fos neurons and LH levels.

claim: Coexpression of POMC-ir was observed in 9.3 ± 2.6% of the Fos-ir neurons of the posterior Arc in the PMv-hit animals.
source: Coexpression of POMC-ir was observed in 9.3 ± 2.6% (12.3 ± 5.0 neurons) of the Fos-ir neurons of the posterior Arc in the PMv-hit animals and 9.6 ± 3.1% (2.3 ± 1.3 neurons) in the hM3Dq clozapine animals.
evidence: This is a direct report of quantitative data from immunohistochemistry analysis.

claim: About 50% of POMC-/Fos-ir neurons also coexpressed mCherry-ir in the PMv-hit animals.
source: Of these POMC-/Fos-ir neurons, about 50% also coexpressed mCherry-ir (7.3 ± 3.2 neurons) in the PMv-hit animals, but almost none in the hM3Dq clozapine animals (0.3 ± 0.3 neurons, Figure 3E–G).
evidence: This is a direct report of quantitative data from immunohistochemistry analysis.

claim: Contamination of POMC neurons may have only mild (if any) contribution to the higher increases in LH observed in some animals.
source: The small number of mCherry/Fos-ir neurons suggests that contamination of POMC neurons may have only mild (if any) contribution to the higher increases in LH observed in some animals, but it is not determinant for inducing LH release.
evidence: This is inferred from the small number of POMC neurons activated.

claim: Contamination of POMC neurons is not determinant for inducing LH release.
source: The small number of mCherry/Fos-ir neurons suggests that contamination of POMC neurons may have only mild (if any) contribution to the higher increases in LH observed in some animals, but it is not determinant for inducing LH release.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that clozapine animals with minimal POMC contamination still showed LH increase.

claim: Only about 10% of Arc Kiss1 (KNDy) neurons of female mice coexpress LepR.
source: We and others have previously shown that only about 10% of Arc Kiss1 (KNDy) neurons of female mice coexpress LepR (Cravo et al., 2013; Donato et al., 2011; Louis et al., 2011; True et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Only 2.5 ± 0.95% of Fos-ir neurons in the posterior Arc were also Kiss1hrGFP positive in LeprCre; Kiss1hrGFP mice following AAV-hM3Dq injections in the PMv.
source: In these animals, only 2.5 ± 0.95% of Fos-ir neurons in the posterior Arc were also Kiss1hrGFP positive (1.8 ± 0.3 neurons), and most of these expressed mCherry, suggesting that one or two KNDy neurons were directly activated by the virus.
evidence: This is a direct report of quantitative data from immunohistochemistry analysis.

claim: The increase in LH does not require KNDy neuronal activation.
source: The low numbers of KNDy neurons expressing Fos-ir in Kiss1hrGFP PMv-hit mice indicates the increase in LH does not require KNDy neuronal activation (Figure 3H–J) in agreement with previous studies from our group showing that direct leptin action in Kiss1 neurons is neither required nor sufficient for puberty and reproduction (Cravo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the low number of activated KNDy neurons and supported by prior research.

claim: Direct leptin action in Kiss1 neurons is neither required nor sufficient for puberty and reproduction.
source: The low numbers of KNDy neurons expressing Fos-ir in Kiss1hrGFP PMv-hit mice indicates the increase in LH does not require KNDy neuronal activation (Figure 3H–J) in agreement with previous studies from our group showing that direct leptin action in Kiss1 neurons is neither required nor sufficient for puberty and reproduction (Cravo et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Virtually no Slc17a6 expression was noticed in LepRb neurons of LeprΔVglut2 mice.
source: As observed in a previous publication (Tong et al., 2007), virtually no Slc17a6 expression was noticed in LepRb neurons of LeprΔVglut2 mice (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: Adult LeprΔVglut2 mice (13–26 weeks old) developed late-onset obesity.
source: Adult LeprΔVglut2 mice (13–26 weeks old) developed late-onset obesity (Figure 4E, F) due to increased fat mass in both sexes (Figure 4G, H), reproducing the metabolic phenotype described before for these animals (Xu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by body weight data shown in Figure 4E-F.

claim: Adult LeprΔVglut2 mice developed late-onset obesity due to increased fat mass in both sexes.
source: Adult LeprΔVglut2 mice (13–26 weeks old) developed late-onset obesity (Figure 4E, F) due to increased fat mass in both sexes (Figure 4G, H), reproducing the metabolic phenotype described before for these animals (Xu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by body composition data shown in Figure 4G-H.

claim: Female LeprΔVglut2 and control LeprCre littermates had similar age of vaginal opening.
source: Female LeprΔVglut2 and control LeprCre littermates had similar age of vaginal opening and showed no differences in body weight at puberty onset (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The day of first estrus was delayed in LeprΔVglut2 mice.
source: The day of first estrus, however, was delayed in LeprΔVglut2 mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: No differences in body weight were observed at vaginal opening and first estrus between experimental and control groups.
source: Of note, no differences in body weight were observed at vaginal opening (puberty onset) and first estrus (puberty completion) between experimental and control groups (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B and 5D.

claim: No differences in age at BPS were found between LeprCre and LeprΔVglut2 male littermates.
source: In males, balanopreputial separation (BPS) was monitored from P25 as a sign of advancement of sexual maturation. No differences in age at BPS were found between LeprCre and LeprΔVglut2 littermates (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: LeprΔVglut2 male mice showed larger body weight than LeprCre mice at the time of BPS.
source: LeprΔVglut2 male mice showed larger body weight than LeprCre mice at the time of BPS (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Length of estrous cycles was longer in LeprΔVglut2 mice compared to controls.
source: Length of estrous cycles was longer (10–16 weeks of age, before the difference in body weight, Figure 5G–I) and the number of cycles completed in 30 days was lower in LeprΔVglut2 mice compared to controls (LeprCre: 4.47 ± 0.30 cycles; LeprΔVglut2: 3.31 ± 0.36 cycles; t26 = 2.45; p = 0.021).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: The number of cycles completed in 30 days was lower in LeprΔVglut2 mice compared to controls.
source: Length of estrous cycles was longer (10–16 weeks of age, before the difference in body weight, Figure 5G–I) and the number of cycles completed in 30 days was lower in LeprΔVglut2 mice compared to controls (LeprCre: 4.47 ± 0.30 cycles; LeprΔVglut2: 3.31 ± 0.36 cycles; t26 = 2.45; p = 0.021).
evidence: This is a direct report of quantitative data with statistical analysis.

claim: Female LeprΔvglut2 spent similar time in estrus, less time in proestrus and more time in diestrus.
source: Female LeprΔvglut2 spent similar time in estrus, less time in proestrus and more time in diestrus (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: 75% of LeprΔVglut2 against 100% of control mice produced at least one litter for 60 days since mating.
source: Analysis of female fertility showed that 75% of LeprΔVglut2 against 100% of control mice produced at least one litter for 60 days since mating.
evidence: This is a direct report of fertility data.

claim: No differences were observed in latency to pregnancy between fertile LeprΔVglut2 and control females.
source: Comparing fertile females, no differences were observed in latency to pregnancy (Figure 5K) or in the number of pups in the first litter (LeprCre: 7.86 ± 1.14 pups; LeprΔVglut2: 7.50 ± 1.41 pups; t11 = 0.20; p = 0.85).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: No differences were observed in the number of pups in the first litter between fertile LeprΔVglut2 and control females.
source: Comparing fertile females, no differences were observed in latency to pregnancy (Figure 5K) or in the number of pups in the first litter (LeprCre: 7.86 ± 1.14 pups; LeprΔVglut2: 7.50 ± 1.41 pups; t11 = 0.20; p = 0.85).
evidence: This is a direct report of quantitative data with statistical analysis.

claim: The disruption in reproductive function in LeprΔVglut2 mice is caused by deficient glutamatergic neurotransmission in LepRb cells, not by metabolic dysregulation.
source: Because delay in first estrus, disruption of the estrous cycles and mild subfertility were observed before differences in body weight appeared (arrow in Figure 4B), our findings indicate that the disruption in reproductive function is caused by deficient glutamatergic neurotransmission in LepRb cells, not by metabolic dysregulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal relationship between reproductive deficits and body weight changes.

claim: LeprΔVglut2 females had denser GnRH-ir fibers in the Arc than Vglut2flox control females.
source: LeprΔVglut2 females had denser GnRH-ir fibers in the Arc than Vglut2flox control females (Figure 6A–C) suggesting retention of the neuropeptide at the neuronal terminals.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: The denser GnRH-ir fibers in the Arc of LeprΔVglut2 females suggests retention of the neuropeptide at the neuronal terminals.
source: LeprΔVglut2 females had denser GnRH-ir fibers in the Arc than Vglut2flox control females (Figure 6A–C) suggesting retention of the neuropeptide at the neuronal terminals.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased GnRH-ir density.

claim: Basal LH levels of diestrous females were not different between LeprΔVglut2 and control genotypes.
